blocks.text: Thermohaline circulation, often called the global conveyor belt, is a crucial process in the Earth's oceans that transports heat from the tropical regions to the poles. It is driven by differences in water temperature and salinity, which together set the density of seawater. Warm, less dense water near the equator moves along the surface towards the polar regions, carrying heat. In polar areas the water cools and becomes denser, because of its lower temperature and the increased salinity from sea-ice formation, so it sinks and flows back towards the equator at deep ocean levels. This continuous movement helps regulate the Earth's climate, influences atmospheric patterns, and supports marine ecosystems by redistributing heat and nutrients globally.

In Fig 21.15, warm surface currents (red) flow poleward, where cooling and ice formation increase their density so that they sink (blue). This cold, dense water spreads along the ocean floor before eventually rising again in other regions. The complete three-dimensional circulation of this global conveyor belt takes approximately 1000 years to cycle water through all the world's ocean basins, and plays a crucial role in regulating the Earth's climate by redistributing heat and nutrients.

blocks.alt: World map with the global conveyor belt: red ribbons (warm shallow current) flow through the Pacific and Indian Oceans, round southern Africa and north through the Atlantic to the far North Atlantic; blue ribbons (cold deep current) run south through the Atlantic, east along the Southern Ocean, north into the Indian and Pacific Oceans. Legend: Warm shallow current, Cold deep current.

blocks.title: Tidbit
blocks.text: Thermohaline circulation, the 'global conveyor belt', takes about 1000 years to make one full cycle around the globe. If global warming slows it down, Europe could face a mini ice age, even while the rest of the world heats up.
Why does cold, salty water sink and create a deep current, and how does this relate to thermohaline circulation?
